action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left occipital 4.9 cm mass in the cuneus and lingual gyrus with thick irregular ring enhancement, central necrosis, rim restricted diffusion, edema involving the left optic radiation, early obstructive dilatation of the occipital horn and 5 mm rightward midline shift
action_criteria.label: Order MRI brain with and without gadolinium contrast (tumor protocol with DWI, FLAIR, post-contrast T1) to fully characterize the left occipital lesion, define the relationship to visual pathways, mass effect, and surgical planning
action_criteria.rationale: Contrast MRI with diffusion and FLAIR characterizes the lesion, its relation to the visual pathway and its mass effect, and plans the surgical approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.rationale: Perfusion supports a high-grade neoplasm and identifies the most vascular region to sample; tissue decides the diagnosis.

action_criteria.rationale: Spectroscopy supports a high-grade neoplasm and shows infiltration beyond the enhancing margin; tissue decides the diagnosis.

action_criteria.rationale: A necrotic ring-enhancing mass at 67, with a family history of gastric cancer: staging CT excludes an extracranial primary if a solitary metastasis is considered.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: All values normal, including platelets 218 and INR 1.0: no laboratory contraindication to surgery or dexamethasone

action_criteria.rationale: Surgery and corticosteroids are planned; coagulation, platelets, electrolytes, glucose and a group and screen are needed first.

action_criteria.label: Score performance status (Karnofsky and ECOG) at this visit
action_criteria.rationale: The choice between standard and hypofractionated chemoradiotherapy depends on age and Karnofsky performance status (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.label: Order DTI tractography of the left optic radiation before resection
action_criteria.rationale: The edema involves the left optic radiation and the tumor reaches the trigone; tractography shows which fibers remain continuous and plans the approach (EANO 2021).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Integrated diagnosis Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4 with IDH1 R132H negative, ATRX retained, MGMT promoter unmethylated
action_criteria.label: Obtain tissue by maximal safe resection of the left occipital lesion, or stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible, for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis with IDH1 R132H immunohistochemistry, ATRX immunohistochemistry and MGMT promoter methylation
action_criteria.rationale: Surgery is the first option for a resectable glioma and should be as extensive as safely possible (AIOM; EANO 2021). Only tissue establishes the integrated diagnosis and the molecular results that select treatment.

action_criteria.rationale: Dexamethasone affects calcium and bone metabolism in osteopenia, glucose and blood pressure.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform lumbar puncture: the 5 mm midline shift, early obstructive dilatation of the occipital horn and bilateral papilledema create a risk of herniation.
Do not initiate definitive tumor-directed therapy (radiation, temozolomide) before tissue diagnosis and molecular profiling are established
Do not attribute the right homonymous hemianopia to the prior right cataract surgery: a binocular field loss respecting the vertical meridian is retrochiasmal and needs brain imaging.
Do not start prophylactic antiseizure medication: the patient has had no seizure, and AIOM recommends against prophylaxis in brain tumour patients without a seizure history.
required_recommendations: Refer urgently to neurosurgery for maximal safe resection of the left occipital lesion, with preoperative DTI tractography of the optic radiation, with stereotactic biopsy if resection is not safely feasible; send the specimen for an integrated histomolecular diagnosis (WHO CNS5).

Start dexamethasone for symptomatic vasogenic edema (for example 4 mg every 6 to 8 hours after a loading dose when mass effect is marked) at the lowest effective dose, with glucose monitoring and gastric protection, and taper after surgery.
Advise her not to drive: a dense right homonymous hemianopia does not meet the visual field standard for driving.

After the integrated diagnosis, refer to the neuro-oncology multidisciplinary team; for glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype at age 70 or under with KPS 70 or more, radiotherapy 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concomitant and adjuvant temozolomide (Stupp 2005; EANO 2021).

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Mei-Ling Chen is a 67-year-old right-handed retired mathematics teacher with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia who presents for inpatient evaluation after referral from an ophthalmologist. Approximately three weeks ago she began noticing that she was missing objects on her right side: bumping into doorframes, failing to notice food on the right side of her plate, and once nearly stepping into traffic from the right. She initially attributed these symptoms to her prior right eye cataract surgery and sought evaluation by her ophthalmologist. A formal visual field test performed two days prior to admission confirmed a dense right homonymous hemianopia. The ophthalmologist, recognizing this as a field loss in both eyes respecting the vertical meridian, immediately ordered brain imaging. An urgent outpatient non-contrast CT showed a left occipital mass with surrounding hypodensity consistent with edema and approximately 5 mm of rightward midline shift, prompting same-day inpatient admission. On further questioning, the patient reports a four-week history of progressive occipital headaches that are worse in the early morning and have occasionally awakened her from sleep. She treated these initially with over-the-counter acetaminophen with partial relief, and noted they are unlike her prior tension headaches in both location and severity. Her husband corroborates the visual complaints and notes she has been unusually cautious while walking due to the visual loss. She denies nausea, vomiting, weakness, sensory loss, speech difficulty, seizures, or loss of consciousness. She has had no prior cancer diagnoses and no known carcinogen exposures. She lost approximately 2 kg over the past month, which she attributes to reduced appetite in the setting of her headaches. She was admitted directly from the ophthalmology clinic for further workup and neurosurgical evaluation.
